/uk-news/2026/oct/02/charged-alleged-ter.headline: Bedford rail crash: train sped up after red light warning, say investigators
/uk-news/2026/oct/02/charged-alleged-ter.excerpt: The train that ran into the back of another in the Bedford rail crash sped up after the driver received a warning he had passed a red light, rail investigators have reported. The driver of the East Midlands train, who died in the crash in June, acknowledged the automatic warning but did not appear to act after passing a danger signal that was rarely ever red. According to an updated report by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch, the train continued to accelerate before the driver applied the emergency brakes when the stationary train in front came into view. The train, a southbound Luton airport express from Corby, could not stop in time, and the collision killed the driver, 60-year-old Shaun Burton, who was described by his employers as a “dedicated railway professional”. Investigators had been seeking to establish if the automatic warning system (AWS) had worked properly, after an initial report found the train had passed a red signal. The latest interim report published on Thursday concluded that the driver had acknowledged the warning, which had not previously displayed a red light during all of 2026, but continued to accelerate to 76mph. After braking, the train slowed to 49mph before it collided with a stationary Nottingham-London train on the same track. The first train had stopped after braking when an AWS warning incorrectly sounded after passing a green signal.
/uk-news/2026/oct/02/charged-alleged-ter.trail: Driver of East Midlands train, who died in June crash, received automatic warning after passing red light but train continued to accelerate

/uk-news/2026/oct/02/charged-alleged-ter.headline: Prisoners thank Andy Burnham as they leave jail in first wave of early releases
/uk-news/2026/oct/02/charged-alleged-ter.excerpt: Prisoners have thanked Andy Burnham as they celebrated walking free from jail early. The first wave of releases began on Thursday, with 700 offenders walking out across England and Wales under the government’s plan to ease prison overcrowding. Those released from dozens of prisons under the government’s latest early release scheme on Thursday were greeted by huddles of journalists requesting their personal messages for the prime minister. Some offenders said they would soon return to jail, because they had nowhere to live and would breach their licence conditions. It follows the damaging early release scheme under Keir Starmer in 2024 when offenders were photographed holding bottles of champagne while saying: “Big up Starmer”. Among the first releases, a former bus driver turned shoplifter, Michael Bogle, 38, from Brent, north London, stepped into the sunlight outside HMP Wandsworth, a south London prison notable for a string of recent scandals. Having served 78 days in prison after breaching a 32-week suspended sentence for shoplifting, he was released early and was pleased that he had been given a place in a bail hostel in south-east London. Asked for his message to Burnham, he said: “Keep the early release going. It’s good.” Bogle, who has been jailed five separate times for 100 convictions, said he had been driven to shoplift “so he could eat” after being made homeless. Prison was “terrible”, Bogle said, adding that there were “too many drugs”.
/uk-news/2026/oct/02/charged-alleged-ter.trail: Seven hundred offenders from dozens of prisons in England and Wales expected to be freed on Thursday

/uk-news/2026/oct/02/charged-alleged-ter.headline: Charity threatens legal action over two-year NHS wait for ADHD and autism assessments
/uk-news/2026/oct/02/charged-alleged-ter.excerpt: ADHD UK has threatened legal action against an NHS organisation over its decision to impose a minimum two-year wait for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism assessments. In a legal letter to West Yorkshire NHS integrated care board (ICB), seen by the Guardian, the charity alleges that the decision to force patients to wait at least two years for such assessments was unlawful and says it will seek a judicial review if the board fails to reverse the policy. West Yorkshire ICB introduced the two-year minimum wait this year, affecting thousands of people with possible ADHD or autism in Leeds, Bradford, Kirklees, Calderdale and Wakefield. West Yorkshire is not the only ICB to ration access to assessment for neurodiversity. The Guardian revealed last week that it was one of four – alongside Devon, Somerset, and North East and North Cumbria – to have imposed minimum waits amid spiralling costs due to the volume of assessments being sought. A further 11 have introduced other mechanisms to ration the number of assessments. ADHD UK claims West Yorkshire failed to follow correct procedures, alleging the ICB breached equalities legislation, denied patients their legal right to choose non-NHS care, failed to involve patients, carers or the public in the decision, and that the decision ran counter to NHS contract regulations.
/uk-news/2026/oct/02/charged-alleged-ter.trail: Exclusive: ADHD UK may seek judicial review of West Yorkshire NHS integrated care board’s ‘unlawful’ policy

/uk-news/2026/oct/02/charged-alleged-ter.headline: Prisoners freed early in England and Wales risk living on the streets, say probation officers
/uk-news/2026/oct/02/charged-alleged-ter.excerpt: Hundreds of prisoners are due to be released early from jail on Thursday amid warnings that many will have nowhere to live and the probation system will struggle to monitor them. About 2,000 criminals including domestic abusers and violent offenders are to be freed over the next month, with another 3,000 in stages over the next year to ease overcrowding. The number was reduced from 6,000 after an intervention by the prime minister, Andy Burnham. Prisoners are supposed to be found appropriate accommodation before their release, significantly reducing reoffending rates. But a probation source told the Guardian that their colleagues in some towns and cities were struggling to find hostel places. “We have a handful of places for ex-offenders and they are full. We are now looking at releasing some people straight on to the street,” the source said. Enver Solomon, the chief executive of the social justice charity Nacro, said: “We know that leaving prison homeless can put people on a path back into custody. It is vital that the whole system from prisons and probation to councils and community providers work together to give people a roof over their heads.” Napo, the probation officers’ union, has raised the issue of the accommodation shortage with prison bosses. The task of finding beds for prisoners is expected to reach critical levels from 13 October, when a second tranche of prisoners is due for release.
/uk-news/2026/oct/02/charged-alleged-ter.trail: Warning of a lack of hostel places for 2,000 criminals due to be released over the next month to ease overcrowding

/education/2026/oct/02/school-inspection.headline: Ofsted drops ‘clumsy’ and ‘offensive’ guidance linking autism and extremism
/education/2026/oct/02/school-inspection.excerpt: Ofsted, the body responsible for safeguarding in education in England, has dropped guidance for inspectors that linked autism and extremism after an outcry from campaigners. An education minister has disclosed that an updated training document “no longer includes reference to children with autism” after claims that it was “offensive” and “clumsy” discrimination. It follows demonstrations involving the naturalist Chris Packham and the comedians Paul Whitehouse and Johnny Vegas and comes amid deepening concerns over the number of autistic children who have been referred to Prevent, the government’s deradicalisation programme. Dr Mine Conkbayir MBE, the researcher and early years specialist who led the campaign, called the decision “fantastic news”. In a social media post she wrote: “Autistic children are not threats. They are children.” The Guardian disclosed a year ago that a document used to teach hundreds of inspectors said that autistic children are “at increased risk of being susceptible to extremism” and “can be drawn into extremism”. Entitled Inspection Safeguarding Session – Prevent Extract 2024, the document, first identified by the human rights group Rights & Security International, said: “Children and young people with autism are at increased risk of being susceptible to extremism. This is because they are more likely to develop special interests.

/politics/2026/oct/02/burnham-law-pensio.headline: Recent lobbyist for Palantir had key role in helping Andy Burnham become PM
/politics/2026/oct/02/burnham-law-pensio.excerpt: A recent lobbyist for the controversial $450bn US tech company Palantir played a senior role in helping Andy Burnham become prime minister, it has emerged. Martha Dalton, whose company Lodestone worked for Palantir in 2024 and 2025, campaigned for Burnham in the Makerfield byelection that secured his return to parliament. She worked closely with his team on strategic communications and rebuttals, and was among supporters who clapped him into Downing Street in July. Lodestone, which Dalton co-founded, worked for Palantir on projects including promoting its software at events in parliament where its engineers demonstrated AI-powered systems for use in British public services to MPs. Dalton previously worked on the autumn 2025 deputy leadership campaign for the current education secretary, Lucy Powell, a few months after Lodestone stopped working for Palantir. Her role emerged as Palantir fights to retain its £330m contract with NHS England to run the federated data platform, a national medical data system. Burnham’s government is under pressure to scrap the deal. Campaigners are angry about Palantir’s work for the Israeli military in Gaza and Donald Trump’s ICE immigration crackdown. They have also raised concerns, acknowledged by NHS England’s chief executive, Jim Mackey, that the benefits to public health may not be as significant as has been claimed.
/politics/2026/oct/02/burnham-law-pensio.trail: Exclusive: Martha Dalton worked closely with Burnham’s team on byelection that secured his return to parliament

/politics/2026/oct/02/burnham-law-pensio.headline: ‘Total class act’: Marie-France van Heel is poised to be a very different PM’s wife
/politics/2026/oct/02/burnham-law-pensio.excerpt: Sarah Brown called Gordon her hero, Samantha Cameron insisted David was “incredibly funny”, while Akshata Murty said Rishi was her best friend. When Marie-France van Heel spoke about her husband, Andy Burnham, in a rare public interview a decade ago, she joked that she had noticed his “good looks … and monobrow”. The spousal humanising of a party leader is a well-worn political tool, but van Heel is likely to be a very different prime ministerial partner. The former senior marketing executive is poised to play a more significant role in promoting Britain than any other spouse in the last two decades, stepping up her political engagements after stepping back from her own corporate career. Van Heel has chosen a political adviser to help her navigate the role at home and promote the UK’s interests overseas, the Guardian understands. She has shifted her role at Be.EV, an electric vehicle-charging network based in Manchester, quitting her job as chief customer officer to give her schedule more flexibility, while remaining on the company’s board. While it is standard for the partners of prime ministers to have taxpayer-funded office support, van Heel has taken on a former special adviser to a cabinet member and is expected to play a more significant role behind the scenes than the previous prime minister Keir Starmer’s wife, Victoria, who continued her work in occupational health for the NHS throughout her husband’s tenure.
/politics/2026/oct/02/burnham-law-pensio.trail: The former marketing executive is expected to play a big role in promoting the UK and could be the most influential spouse in No 10 in years

/politics/2026/oct/02/burnham-law-pensio.headline: Burnham’s reopening of Brexit debate is ‘biggest boost in my career’, says Farage
/politics/2026/oct/02/burnham-law-pensio.excerpt: Nigel Farage has claimed that Andy Burnham has given him “the biggest boost in my career” by reviving the Brexit debate, which the Reform UK leader said had reopened a “huge flank” to his party. The prime minister’s pledges to the Labour conference and admission on Wednesday that rejoining the EU was among options the government would look at had put “put me back into the debate”, he said. Looking tanned and relaxed before his party’s first major rally since its conference last month, Farage indicated to reporters that he was relishing a return to the playbook that he and others deployed during the 2016 referendum. Dismissing polls showing that as much as 59% of the public favoured rejoining the EU, Farage told the Guardian: “Of course they do, until you tell them it’ll cost 25bn quid a year, until you tell him it’ll mean joining Schengen [the area of Europe that has open borders], until he tells them it will mean actually having to recommit to joining the euro. “Remember that the leavers haven’t made their arguments since 2016. The ‘remoaners’ have made their arguments every single week. I mean, do you know what? I actually think that Burnham has made a very big political mistake here.” Farage was speaking before a rally in the South Yorkshire city of Doncaster, the first of a series Reform is holding around Britain on the theme of what the party would do in its first 100 days of government.
/politics/2026/oct/02/burnham-law-pensio.trail: Reform UK leader tells supporters PM’s move has ‘opened up a huge flank to us’

/world/2026/oct/02/aviation-security-fly.headline: Australian couple on plane diverted after flydubai co-pilot’s alleged attack on pilot
/world/2026/oct/02/aviation-security-fly.excerpt: Two Australian citizens onboard a flight to Tel Aviv that was diverted after one of the pilots allegedly stabbed the other in an attack are “safe,” the foreign minister confirmed. The passengers are a Jewish couple from Sydney, the Israeli embassy in Australia confirmed to the Guardian on Thursday. No further details were provided. The flydubai aircraft was travelling from the United Arab Emirates to Israel when it was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. In a post on social media, Penny Wong thanked the “heroes” for thwarting the attack. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “Relieved to confirm at least two Australians who were on the Flydubai flight to Israel are safe – thanks to the heroes who thwarted the attack and helped bring the passengers to safety,” she wrote. “We’re thinking of those injured and hope for their full recovery.” One of the pilots, whom Israeli officials said was an Omani citizen, is accused of stabbing his fellow pilot. During the alleged attack, the plane plunged about 17,000 feet in just two minutes. Passenger Yaniv Hayoun later recounted how he and other passengers heard screaming and felt pressure as the plane dived before forcing their way into the cockpit and finding the attacker at the instrument panel. “I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during a meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel.
/world/2026/oct/02/aviation-security-fly.trail: Two people from Sydney were on board flight to Tel Aviv that was dramatically diverted to Saudi Arabia after one pilot allegedly stabbed the other

/world/2026/oct/02/aviation-security-fly.headline: ‘Hero’ pilot, plumber and dentist among those who saved flydubai flight to Israel
/world/2026/oct/02/aviation-security-fly.excerpt: Smit Machchhar was lying on the floor of the flydubai flight deck, covered in blood, when he managed to click the release to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to gain entry, overpower his attacker and save 174 passengers onboard. Moments earlier, Machchhar’s fellow pilot had stabbed him, in an apparent effort to crash the plane, which was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv. Machchhar, from Mumbai, is being treated in a hospital in Saudi Arabia’s north-western city of Tabuk, where the plane landed safely. The Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, lauded Machchhar as a hero in a post on X early on Thursday. “In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously ‌injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others. His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy,” he wrote. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, was equally impressed with Machchhar’s actions. “Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker,” he said. Machchhar is one of several people hailed as heroes for managing to wrest control of the plane from the attacker who apparently attempted to crash it, according to Israeli officials who also provided much of the detail on how events played out inside the plane.
/world/2026/oct/02/aviation-security-fly.trail: Swift actions of Smit Machchhar allowed passengers and off-duty pilots to subdue attacker and land plane safely

/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.headline: Brazil attorney general says meddling ‘cannot be tolerated’ after Trump funding plans revealed
/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.excerpt: Brazil’s attorney general has said foreign meddling in his country’s institutions and democracy “cannot be tolerated” after a Guardian report revealed how the Trump administration was pushing to direct funds to a campaign against the Brazilian supreme court. Writing on X, Jorge Messias called the report “an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty”. “The information is especially serious in light of Brazil’s electoral process and the recent episodes of external pressure on our institutions,” Messias added. Brazil is three days away from its presidential election – the outcome of which Washington has been accused of trying to influence – where the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, will face off against his far-right rival, the Trump ally Flávio Bolsonaro. The pair are neck and neck in the polls. According to the Brazilian television network GloboNews, the attorney general’s office on Thursday filed a criminal complaint to investigate potential wrongdoing, in response to the Guardian story. Last year, the Trump administration used a campaign of sanctions and tariffs in a failed attempt to pressure Lula’s government and the supreme court over the coup trial of Bolsonaro’s father, the ex-president Jair Bolsonaro. Trump called Bolsonaro’s prosecution a “witch-hunt”, but he was convicted and handed a 27-year sentence for trying to seize power after losing the 2022 election to Lula.
/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.trail: Jorge Messias calls Guardian report ‘an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty’ as nation prepares to go to polls

/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.headline: ‘We’re afraid of dying’: Brazilian news site will not cover upcoming elections after threats
/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.excerpt: Four years ago, during Brazil’s last presidential election, the tyres were slashed on the pickup truck used for reporting by Tapajós de Fato, an independent journalism website in the Brazilian Amazon. Days later, a cat’s severed head was left next to the car park, alongside a note bearing the name of one of the site’s founders, Marcos Wesley Pedroso, and a warning that he would be next. Last July, security cameras outside Pedroso’s house showed cyclists circling the block, whistling and filming his car until, minutes later, another car crashed into it. “I believe they wanted me to come outside so they could ambush me,” said Pedroso. Police have not identified those responsible or established whether the cases are connected, but Pedroso sees them as part of a wider series of threats linked to Tapajós de Fato’s reporting on environmental and Indigenous rights violations, land disputes, and pesticide contamination in the Amazonian state of Pará. As a result, the site’s team decided not to cover this year’s elections – which will choose the next president, state governors, members of the lower house and part of the senate, with the first round on 4 October. “We’re afraid of dying and of putting our families’ safety at risk,” said Pedroso. He added that the site, whose name refers to the 1,238-mile-long (1,992km) Tapajós River, would remain online and continue covering environmental issues, but would avoid stories about the election.
/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.trail: Co-founder of independent website Tapajós de Fato said decision was made to protect journalists and their families

/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.headline: John Oliver on Brazil’s Flávio Bolsonaro: ‘Fearmongering and flagrant daddy issues’
/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.excerpt: On the latest Last Week Tonight, John Oliver looked ahead to Sunday’s major election in Brazil, where 160 million people will vote to determine the country’s president, as well as state governors, two-thirds of the senate and every member of the lower house. “Yet again, Brazil finds itself having to choose between Lula and a guy named Bolsonaro for president, and many do not seem thrilled that those are their main choices,” the host explained of the two candidates for president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, and Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the disgraced former rightwing president Jair Bolsonaro. All signs are pointing toward an extremely close race, “which is worrying, because that means the world’s fourth-largest democracy and the home to, not insignificantly, the rainforest that is key to meeting the world’s climate goals, could yet again be run by a dangerous dipshit named Bolsonaro,” said Oliver. The host then traced how we got to this moment, after Lula defeated Jair Bolsonaro by two percentage points in 2022, the smallest margin for a Brazilian presidential election since the fall of the military dictatorship in 1985. Bolsonaro fled to Florida, but months later, violent rioters clashed with police as they vandalized government buildings, claiming Bolsonaro did not actually lose the election.
/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.trail: The Last Week Tonight host digs into Brazil’s election, with current leader Lula faces a disgraced former president’s son

/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.headline: ‘Viscerally dedicated to social issues’: behind Lula’s drive to win final term in Brazil’s crunch election
/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.excerpt: On 1 January 2023, a few hours after being sworn in for his third stint as Brazil’s president, a ravenous Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva sneaked away from a celebratory cocktail party packed with politicians and diplomats to grab a snack with one of his oldest friends. “This is your penultimate term,” that friend, the Dominican theologian and writer Frei Betto, recalls telling Lula as the pair chewed the fat in a back room of the foreign ministry in Brasília. Betto says Lula laughed off his provocation, insisting: “No, Betto! It’s the last one. I’m done!” But the theologian was unconvinced. “I’m certain that in four years’ time you’ll stand for a fourth,” he assured the leftwing veteran during their 40-minute tête-à-tête. “And sure enough, he did,” Betto added last month, as his forecast came true. On 4 October, just a few weeks shy of his 81st birthday, Lula will indeed seek to extend his legendary five-decade career in what will be the former union leader’s seventh presidential election since his first in 1989. Lula ran three unsuccessful campaigns before finally making history as Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002 and winning re-election in 2006. In 2022 he staged a sensational comeback, defeating the far-right incumbent, Jair Bolsonaro, before thwarting a coup attempt masterminded by his rival a week into his third term.
/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.trail: Longtime friend tells of president’s obsession with social justice and fears for country’s future under another Bolsonaro presidency

/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.headline: Lula says Trump wants to ‘colonise’ and capture Brazil’s resources by meddling in election
/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.excerpt: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s presidential campaign has accused Donald Trump of wanting to “colonise” Brazil in order to capture its natural resources by meddling in next month’s presidential election. The accusation came in a campaign advert that was published on social media on Thursday night by Lula’s team and will air on television on Friday amid growing fears over the impact alleged US interference could have on the vote. The TV spot claims the US president is trying to sway the election in favour of Lula’s far-right adversary in the election, Flávio Bolsonaro, in order to advance Trump’s interests in the South American nation. “Flávio Bolsonaro is Trump’s candidate and what Trump wants is to colonise Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust,” the female narrator tells viewers in the minute-long video. The state department has denied claims the US is meddling in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” it said last month in a statement. Writing on X, Lula accused Bolsonaro of wanting to “hand our natural resources over to the United States”. “If it’s up to him, Brazil will become a colony again,” the incumbent leftwing president added. With just over a week to go until the 4 October first round vote, Lula and Bolsonaro are neck and neck in the polls. A second round run-off will be held on 25 October if no candidate secures more than half of the votes.
/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.trail: A TV spot claims the US president is trying to sway October’s presidential vote in favour of Lula’s far-right opponents

/world/2026/oct/02/student-protests-shut.headline: ‘We swept a lot under the carpet’: Vichy regime film hits home in France of 2026
/world/2026/oct/02/student-protests-shut.excerpt: It is the story of how a lowly state administrator unthinkingly becomes a cog in the machine of an authoritarian regime, embracing the bureaucracy and logistics of sending people to their deaths – and it is drawing in audiences to French cinemas. The French film Notre Salut (Our Salvation), with its modern lighting, improvised scenes and anachronistic 1980s Europop soundtrack, is far from the standard historical costume drama about the second world war. But the award-winning film about the daily lives of ordinary people participating in the puppet Vichy regime that collaborated with the Nazis – and ensured the deportation of a quarter of France’s Jewish population to concentration camps – is poised to become a box office hit. The film, which has been given the English-language title A Man of His Time, had a strong cinema opening in France this week, particularly among young audiences, at a time when the country is soul-searching ahead of next spring’s presidential election. Marine Le Pen of the far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN) continues to top the polls for the presidential race despite the political fallout from an investigation by Mediapart alleging that her party leader, Jordan Bardella, published antisemitic comments as a young party member, which he denies.

/world/2026/oct/02/student-protests-shut.headline: France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting
/world/2026/oct/02/student-protests-shut.excerpt: A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned, as it said many schools would switch to online classes to protect teachers and pupils. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called a crisis cabinet meeting on Thursday and told ministers to cancel travel plans to deal with the demonstrations, which erupted in the Paris region last week but have snowballed across the country. Lecornu’s office said: “This upsurge in violence makes it virtually impossible to maintain the continuity of public education and is exposing staff and students to danger.” The education minister, Édouard Geffray, is to meet pupil representatives on Friday. About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents were under way outside high schools around the country, police said, with more than 160 shut down as a result. Access was also blocked to about 30 university campuses on Thursday, including in Paris and Marseille. Nearly 3,000 lycée students – aged between 15 and 18 – have been detained since the start of the protests, including 1,949 on Thursday alone, the interior ministry said. More than 300 police and dozens of firefighters, teachers and pupils have been injured. The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves earlier this year.
/world/2026/oct/02/student-protests-shut.trail: About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents under way outside high schools around the country

/world/2026/oct/02/student-protests-shut.headline: Why is the UK-France ‘one in, one out’ migration deal being scrapped?
/world/2026/oct/02/student-protests-shut.excerpt: The UK government’s “one in, one out” deal with France, which was supposed to help deter small boat arrivals, is expected to expire on Thursday, government sources have said. What was one in, one out? The deal involved returning to France one asylum seeker who had arrived in the UK in a small boat, in exchange for another brought legally to the UK from France. It lasted 423 days – from 10 July 2025 until 1 October 2026. Why didn’t it work out? The UK’s official explanation was that it had not been able to scale up the numbers of asylum seekers involved as much as it would have liked to. However, the scheme was beset with problems. Scores returned to the UK during the scheme because they felt unsafe in France. Some were returned to France a second time while others were allowed to remain in the UK to have their claims processed here. Many were believed to have vanished after being returned to France. Asylum seekers said they were threatened by smugglers because they owed them money and feared being sent back to their home countries or to another European country they had passed through on their journey. How many people were sent back under it and how many returned to the UK? Approximately 1,500 asylum seekers were returned to France, with a similar number brought legally from France to the UK. The numbers removed under the scheme were fewer than the total who arrived in small boats over seven days in the second half of last month.
/world/2026/oct/02/student-protests-shut.trail: Agreement expected to end on Thursday after running for 423 days, during which it has been beset by problems

/world/2026/oct/02/student-protests-shut.headline: Stella McCartney makes waves with ‘sea life, not sea food’ theme in zero-wool Paris show
/world/2026/oct/02/student-protests-shut.excerpt: Stella McCartney has been talking about animal rights at fashion week for 30 years. She is usually a lone voice, but the issue is back in the headlines this season. Outcry over the physical restraining of a Peta protester at a catwalk show by Steven Kolb, the president of New York fashion week’s governing body, has put cruelty in wool production – previously considered niche compared to the hot button topic of fur – on the news agenda. “There is no wool on the runway this season, and I’m proud of that,” McCartney said after her show. She has been working on wool alternatives, including Brewed Protein, a fermented alternative to cashmere and wool developed in collaboration with the Japanese biotech firm Spiber, which was first used in her collections a year ago. The issue, she says, is “a tricky one. I’ve got alpacas at home, and I have to shear them. If you can shear a sheep in a kind, humane way, then I don’t, personally, think that’s the end of the world. When we do have wool in our collections it is responsibly sourced. But the way a lot of [wool production] is done today is deeply cruel. “At the end of the day it’s about how kind you are, but monitoring that kindness requires real work. At Stella, we police everything from start to finish at my cost, at my time. If I use wool, I can show you exactly where it’s coming from, and I’m proud of that.
/world/2026/oct/02/student-protests-shut.trail: Designer showcases wool alternatives and ocean-inspired clothes and says ‘kindness requires real work’

/world/2026/oct/02/student-protests-shut.headline: Macron says ‘welcome back’ to Burnham suggestion UK could rejoin EU
/world/2026/oct/02/student-protests-shut.excerpt: The French president, Emmanuel Macron, has reacted warmly to Andy Burnham’s suggestion that the UK could rejoin the EU. “Welcome back,” the French leader said in English with a smile at a news conference in Madrid on Wednesday. Macron continued in French: “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.” Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said his country would open its arms to any bid from the UK to rejoin the EU. The two leaders were responding to the British prime minister’s speech at the Labour party conference in which Burnham said Britain would not have a clear path “until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market” and that Brexit had “done more harm than good”. In a series of interviews on Wednesday, Burnham said the government could maintain the status quo, seek a customs union, return to the single market or “go all the way” for full EU membership. Macron said the British had “always been useful in helping us simplify things” when the UK was part of the EU and were “demanding partners”. Burnham “is right to have this boldness”, he added. Earlier, Macron, who has frequently accused the proponents of Brexit of misleading the public, said Brexit had been “the biggest lie of the last 30 years”, pointing to shortfalls in promised economic growth and trade opportunities.
